Structural Injustice as Emergent Disorder HOCHAN KIM Bates College, United States S

tructural injustice remains a puzzling concept despite its increasing prominence. I distill recent theoretical challenges into a dilemma: either structural injustice lacks the normative credentials of injustice given that wrongdoing is inessential, or it is redundant given existing theories that trace injustice to culpable state and other institutional failures. I thendevelop a novel account of structural injustice, the Complexity View, that unravels this dilemma. The emergent properties of human actions in a complex society explain what is “structural” about structural injustice, specifically how it can arise without (culpable) wrongdoing. Structural injustice is unjust because it is wrong to contribute to social processes that cause harm and to passively accept preventable forms of vulnerability and deprivation as tragic misfortunes. But this account of structural injustice has a sobering implication: while complexity explains what distinguishes structural injustice from other wrongs, it also sets significant epistemic limits on social reform.

INTRODUCTION S

tructural injustice has become a prominent topic in contemporary political theory. In contrast to wrongs found in interpersonal interactions or the policies of a repressive state, Iris Marion Young (2011) argues in her pathbreaking account, structural injustice is a wrong that lies in the cumulative constraining and enabling effects of social structures in the backdrop of people’s lives, effects that significantly harm certain groups. These effects, she argues, are produced by complex social processes driven by the actions, not necessarily wrongful, of many people pursuing legitimate goals within the existing framework of rules and resources. By broadening our normative focus from individual and institutional wrongdoings toward unjust yet often ignored forms of vulnerability and deprivation within our social structures, the concept of structural injustice aims to illuminate a distinctive and pressing problem in contemporary society for social criticism and political redress. Yet the concept of structural injustice continues to generate theoretical puzzlement and disagreement. Two recent criticisms of Young’s account bring out one important puzzle. For some critics, we should be skeptical that these sorts of problems count as an injustice in the first place. Plausibly, what distinguishes injustice from mere tragedy or misfortune is its origin in the wrongful conduct of human agents, conduct that warrants moral grievances like anger or indignation (Estlund 2024). It is unclear whether something that occurs without any wrongdoing has the normative credentials of injustice. Thus, these critics ask, if structural injustice is not necessarily the result of anyone

doing anything wrong, why should our attitude toward it be any different than our attitude toward natural disasters and their terrible, but not wrongful, effects? The question is not specific to the concept of structural injustice but applies more broadly to cognates ideas like structural racism as “racism without racists” (Bonilla- Silva 2003) or capitalism as an inherently unjust economic structure (Cordelli 2025). Any structural theory of injustice must answer the question: given that wrongdoing is inessential, what’s unjust about structural injustice? Other critics have questioned the purported distinction between structural injustice and institutional wrongdoing. A wave of recent accounts argues that institutional wrongdoing plays a central role in structural injustice (Mantouvalou 2023; McKeown 2024; Nuti 2019; Powers and Faden 2019). According to Maeve McKeown, Young mistakenly focused on conceptualizing “pure” structural injustice involving no wrongdoing whatsoever. In reality, most if not all structural injustices are “deliberate” or “avoidable” wrongs perpetrated by the powerful institutional agents like the state. Homelessness, McKeown (2024, 41–2) argues about one of Young’s core examples, can and should be addressed by the state through measures like implementing rent control and building more public housing; that affluent states have largely failed to do so is a serious wrongdoing on their part. Far from being conceptually distinct from institutional wrongdoing, these accounts argue, structural injustice is a problem perpetrated largely by the wrongdoings of powerful institutions. Together, these criticisms reveal a significant tension within the concept of structural injustice. As a claim of injustice, it looks normatively suspect unless it can be tethered to agential wrongdoing. Pointing to institutional wrongdoing, as recent accounts do, would seem to dispel such suspicions. But as some responses to these accounts have started to point out (Browne 2025; De Bernardi 2024; Marin 2024), the resulting view threatens to deflate what made the concept distinctive in the first place: that there is something about social structures, separate from the wrongdoings of

specific and even quite powerful agents, that is crucial for understanding and redressing certain injustices in contemporary society. To put this point more sharply, once institutions like states and corporations are understood to be agents in their own right (List and Pettit 2011), the concept of structural injustice appears redundant: there already exist theories of justice and injustice that trace injustices in contemporary society to institutions like the state as powerful agents that wield enormous influence over social outcomes, and it is unclear what, if anything, the concept of structural injustice adds to these theories. Some may welcome this deflationary conclusion. But the thought that the concept of structural injustice names a distinct problem in contemporary society from both individual and institutional wrongdoing remains attractive to many, even as its theoretical difficulties have become increasingly clear. This article develops a novel account of what structural injustice is and why it is unjust, and in doing so, offers a solution to this puzzle. I call this account the Complexity View. What is distinctively “structural” about structural injustice is its basis in the emergent properties of human actions in society, understood as a kind of complex system. Many harmful social outcomes are not straightforwardly reducible to or predictable from features of the agents who bring them about; indeed, these outcomes often run contrary to what any of those agents intended. This counterintuitive relationship between action and outcome in a complex society explains how structural injustice comes apart from wrongdoing (or at least culpable wrongdoing) and why it cannot be chalked up to faulty institutions. What is unjust about structural injustice is explained by two moral considerations: the wrongfulness of agents causing harm to others even when that harm was unintended and unforeseeable, and the wrongfulness of agents passively resigning themselves to harmful emergent outcomes that are preventable through political intervention and social reform. In these ways, structural injustice has the normative credentials of injustice. If successful, the Complexity View shows that the concept of structural injustice is both plausible and valuable. It illuminates how human actions can create emergent forms of vulnerability and deprivation in a complex society, while also issuing a reminder that these problems are neither natural disasters nor invulnerable to political redress. That said, this account comes with a sobering implication for how agents can and should politically respond to these problems: the very same issue of complexity that essentially distinguishes structural injustice from other wrongs also creates significant, though surmountable, epistemic barriers for the pursuit of deliberate and effective social reform.

THE DILEMMA FOR STRUCTURAL INJUSTICE

To begin making the central puzzle more concrete, consider a widely discussed example from Young (2011, 43–4): the case of Sandy, a single mother and commuter in a typical American city who ends up facing homelessness when her current apartment

building is sold to a developer, setting off a chain of events in which various structural constraints produced by the actions of countless others—from the price and availability of housing in her city to the quality of schools in different neighborhoods—prevent her from finding a new residence, leaving her on the verge of homelessness. As Young sets up the case, no one treats Sandy wrongly during this ordeal. Nonetheless, Sandy finds herself facing a common and, Young argues, unjust situation. It is unjust that anyone should face the prospect of homelessness, especially in an affluent society. Sandy experiences a structural injustice, and this is a distinct phenomenon from agential wrongdoing. Many have found Young’s description of Sandy’s situation compelling. Others have different reactions. One is that Sandy’s situation is surely the product of at least one (collective) agent’s wrongdoing: her state. Her state should be doing more to ensure that Sandy and others like her are not vulnerable to homelessness; it bears responsibility for her situation. Another is that Sandy’s situation is not an injustice, however unfortunate it may be, given that it is not the result of anyone having wronged her in any way. Of course, she is entitled to some help to get back on her feet—but that is a matter of human decency or charity, not a matter of her having suffered an injustice. These reactions correspond to what I call the redundancy challenge and the normative challenge, respectively. The redundancy challenge says the concept of structural injustice is unnecessary: everything we want to say with the concept of structural injustice can and should be said in terms of individual and collective wrongdoings. The normative challenge says the concept of structural injustice is implausible: to the extent that it is essentially about something other than agential wrongdoing, it lacks the normative credentials to be an injustice. Despite their important insights, existing accounts of structural injustice are vulnerable to at least one of these challenges. Young’s account is vulnerable to the normative challenge. She maintains that structural injustice is distinct from individual and institutional wrongdoing, but she does not offer an alternative explanation of why it is unjust and not merely tragic. Situations like Sandy’s, she suggests, are obviously unjust. But this is not a satisfactory answer to the normative challenge, as David Estlund (2024) has recently argued. For any situation that seems obviously unjust, he asks, suppose that the exact same situation had been produced by an unpreventable natural disaster like a hurricane. Such occurrences are commonly considered tragedies, not injustices. The relevant difference between the two is a moral, specifically a deontic, fact: unpreventable natural disasters are not a matter of anyone having treated others wrongly, indeed not a matter of human action at all.1 What plausibly

distinguishes an unjust state of affairs from a merely tragic one is its basis in the wrongful conduct of agents, conduct that licenses moral grievances like anger or indignation on the part of the victims. According to Young’s description, Sandy’s situation is not unjust in this sense. It is not a matter of anyone having treated her wrongly. Of course, Sandy’s situation differs from a hurricane insofar as it is the product of human action, specifically the actions of many agents interacting in the housing market. But the point of the hurricane analogy is precisely that there is no discernible morally significant difference between these two scenarios. Recent accounts of structural injustice appear less vulnerable to the normative challenge (Mantouvalou 2023; McKeown 2024; Nuti 2019; Powers and Faden 2019). Departing from Young, they argue that structural injustice is, at least in large part, the product of wrongdoings by the state and other powerful collective or corporate agents. In McKeown’s (2024, 181 and 44) words, “powerful corporate agents like states and corporations can be held morally responsible for structural injustice, either by omission (avoidable structural injustice) or action (deliberate structural injustice)” because “powerful agents have the capacity to change the situation, [but] they actively maintain it. So the consequences are not unintentional, they are intentional.” Sandy would not be facing homelessness if her state took action, such as improving tenants’ rights and implementing rent control. By failing to implement such measures now and in the past, her state bears responsibility for her situation. Once the role of these powerful collective agents is acknowledged, the claim that structural injustice is distinct from wrongdoing looks less plausible and, in any case, irrelevant to understanding injustices here and now. Importantly, these accounts do not completely part ways with Young’s account. They maintain that individuals are not culpable for their part in structural injustice, because the conduct of ordinary individuals is not “where the action is, both in terms of understanding structural stability or change and in attributing responsibility for structural injustice” (McKeown 2024, 36–7). Structural injustice is primarily the product of wrongful institutional conduct. Call this the Institutional View of structural injustice. The Institutional View seems to offer a straightforward answer to the normative challenge: structural injustice is unjust because it is traceable to the wrongful conduct of powerful collective agents. Sandy’s situation is not a tragedy; it is a deliberate or avoidable injustice perpetrated by her state, real estate corporations, and other powerful institutions. A closer examination, however, reveals some problems with this answer. The trouble lies in the Institutional View’s ambiguous stance on whether structural injustice is simply a product of collective agents’ wrongdoing or whether it is in fact the product of a much broader and complicated set of human actions involving, crucially, ordinary individuals. Is structural injustice ultimately the product of collective agents’ wrongdoings, or is it only largely the product of such wrongdoings (and if so, how large)?

Take patriarchy as an example. Estlund (2024, 353) writes, “The many instances of individual behavior that together produce a patriarchal social structure…are, in large part even if not entirely, acts that are uncoordinated across strangers.” Here he challenges, rightly, the Institutional View’s claim that the conduct of ordinary individuals is not “where the action is” for structural injustice. Social structures like patriarchy are not just what powerful institutions do. Sharon Krause (2013, 194) recounts a memorable example of how social processes like gender socialization among individuals play an important role in patriarchy’s reproduction: “When I was a girl my mother was constantly enjoining me to ‘take smaller steps’ so as to be more ‘ladylike’. Apparently, my natural stride was too long, perhaps too forceful, to be feminine….[H]er exhortations, intended as loving guidance, did have the effect of socializing me to norms that subtly perpetuate inequalities between men and women.” Pointing to group agents thus offers only a partial answer to the normative challenge. To establish the deontic wrongness of structural injustice, the actions of many other agents must be normatively accounted for. Defenders of the Institutional View could respond in two ways. One response is to move further away from Young’s account and say that ordinary individuals, not just states and corporations, are guilty of wrongdoing when their actions contribute to structural injustice.2 This would provide a full answer to the normative challenge. But this move is not available to the Institutional View given its central commitment to the uniquely wrongful role of powerful institutions for problems of structural injustice. More importantly, to say that individuals are also guilty for contributing to structural injustice and simply leaving the matter there would be to miss one of the important points of Krause’s example. Ordinary individuals do contribute to structural injustices like patriarchy, but the nature of their contribution is not always something that licenses guilt or blame. Krause (2013, 195) writes, “The truth is that we participate all the time in practices that subordinate us even as they perpetuate the domination of others, and much of the time these acts of subordination and domination are neither recognized as such nor intended, much less controlled.” Socializing one’s child into certain gender norms is now seen by many as wrongful: as Krause’s own reflections demonstrate, people have come to understand that this practice perpetuates gender inequality and stifles individual freedom. This understanding may have innocently eluded Krause’s mother who, Krause observes, was well intentioned and in many ways a victim of patriarchy herself. A different response that preserves the Institutional View’s core commitment is this: when individuals’ actions contribute to structural injustice, it is the state that bears responsibility for those actions. It is part of the state’s power, the Institutionalist can argue, to regulate individual conduct that leads to injustices like Sandy’s situation. Inadequate public regulation enables private actors to act in ways that create, exacerbate, and exploit certain forms of structural vulnerability (Mantouvalou 2023). The state should intervene to ensure that uncoordinated acts across strangers do not lead to harm. These are not uncontroversial claims. Some may worry about the compatibility of such interventions with liberal limits on state power over individual choices, especially related to injustices like patriarchy; others may worry about their effectiveness, especially given those limits but even without them. For now, let us set these worries aside—after all, these worries may be overblown, and theorists of structural injustice need not be wedded to liberalism—and grant that the state has legitimate and effective power to regulate individual conduct in ways that would address structural injustice. This would provide a complete yet resolutely institutionalist answer to the normative challenge. The normative credentials of structural injustice are found in the wrongdoing of powerful institutions, both for their own conduct and that of individuals. But now the redundancy challenge rears its head. The Institutional View, so understood, threatens to make the concept of structural injustice theoretically redundant, or at least significantly deflates what appeared interesting and distinctive about it. Much work in political theory has already argued for the view that social injustices are rooted in powerful institutions like the state and their profound and pervasive influence on people’s lives, what John Rawls (1999) calls the “basic structure of society.” If structural injustice should be understood as a deliberate or avoidable wrong committed by powerful institutions, is it not just a species of institutional wrongdoing after all? What is gained, theoretically or politically, by calling Sandy’s situation a structural injustice rather than an institutional failure if the problem simply lies in her state’s unjust housing policies? The same can be asked about other issues like global poverty, which McKeown (2024, 102) claims is an avoidable structural injustice because “international institutions and powerful states have the capacity to change the structures that underlie global poverty”—a familiar argument in the literature on global (distributive) justice (see, e.g., Pogge 2002). The Institutional View has the resources to fully answer the normative challenge, but in doing so, it collapses structural injustice into the familiar question of institutional justice (Browne 2025, 31; De Bernardi 2024). Some may argue that this is exactly the right way to think about structural injustice and what is “structural” about it. Social structure, in their view, is fundamentally about institutional design, how “the rules of the game in a society” (North 1990, 3) set by institutions like the state channel human interactions in a certain direction. But there are plausible views in social and political

theory that maintain that the idea of social structure encompasses much more than institutional rules. Indeed, for Young, that is precisely the point of conceptualizing structural injustice. Drawing on insights from social theorists such as Pierre Bourdieu (1977) and Anthony Giddens (1984), she insists that the concept identifies a phenomenon that is generally overlooked by theories of justice that analyze social structure by examining the state and other formal institutions. Taking a truly structural perspective on injustice requires “looking at the whole society” and the social processes driven by the actions of all agents within it, not just looking at a small institutional subset of that society that is assumed to be “more fundamental” (or more powerful) than the rest (Young 2011, 70).3 Examples of such processes include the normalization of a dominant racial or ethnic group’s cultural values and habits, the reproduction of the gendered division of labor in households, and, as Krause reminds us, the transmission of gendered bodily comportment to children. Undoubtedly, these processes are significantly influenced by what institutions do. But it would be a serious mistake to assume that these social processes can simply be placed under institutional control or that the individual behaviors driving these processes can be read off from the institutional framework of rules in which they occur, absent further facts about culture, norms, bodies, etc. To my eye, this broader understanding of social structure is crucial for a nonredundant conceptualization of structural injustice. It is what makes the concept novel and interesting, theoretically and politically. The trouble with the Institutional View is that it gives up this important insight in its understandable quest to hold powerful institutions morally responsible for structural injustice. It claims, or must claim in response to the normative challenge, that certain institutions are the more powerful, fundamental part of society—“where the action is”—to maintain that structural injustice is the result of wrongful institutional conduct while ignoring the actions of ordinary individuals and exempting them from similar moral evaluation. The theoretical cost of this move is to make the concept of structural injustice redundant. Any so-called structural injustice could be fully redescribed in terms of institutional wrongdoing. At best, the concept of structural injustice would serve as a stepping stone for filling some overlooked gap in the theory of institutional justice, but once that theory is filled out, it would say everything the concept was meant to capture. Together, these challenges pose a dilemma for the concept of structural injustice. The more that structural injustice is untethered from agential wrongdoing, the less it looks like a genuine injustice, rather than a tragedy that is morally indistinct from a natural disaster. Yet the more that structural injustice is grounded in institutional or some other wrongdoing, the less novel and interesting the concept turns out to be. On one

Either Sandy’s situation is a product of her state or some other agent wronging her, but then it no longer needs to be called a “structural” injustice; or her situation is not a matter of anyone wronging her, but then the label of structural “injustice” looks unwarranted. But how could that be?

EMERGENCE, COMPLEXITY, AND SPONTANEOUS ORDER

This section begins developing an account of structural injustice that unravels this puzzle, building on Young’s important but underdeveloped thought that structural injustice is a product of complex social processes driven, in large part, by ordinary individuals and their actions. A major step toward this account is taken in Sally Haslanger’s (2022; 2023) recent work in social ontology, which integrates ideas from social theory and philosophy into an original theory of society as a complex dynamic system structured by the social practices of individuals. One notable passage reads: “Societies are not planned and implemented by anyone. They are self-organizing systems. Although legislatures, economists, planning boards, and policy makers undertake to construct and intervene in social systems, and what they do matters, they are not in control. The society, so to speak, has a life of its own, and much of what happens is not designed or intended by anyone” (Haslanger 2023, 9). This is a strikingly different picture of society from the Institutional View. Here, the state (and other powerful institutions) is but one agent among many in the system, and as comparatively powerful as it may be, it is not “in control” of the society it aims to manage. Why not? Consider the issue of racial residential segregation, “the linchpin” (Massey 2020) of racial inequality in the United States as a problem of structural injustice. It is now widely recognized that ending legally enforced or de jure segregation has not addressed de facto segregation: a recent study finds that most metropolitan areas were more racially segregated in 2019 than they were in 1990 (Menendian, Gambhir, and Gailes 2021). Part of the explanation for this is a history of culpable discriminatory practices by political, financial, and real estate institutions, such as redlining, that have only recently been outlawed. But it would be a mistake to attribute the persistence of residential segregation to institutional actors alone. Residential segregation is also driven by social processes that the state does not control, most notably the choices of many individuals navigating the housing market. Thus, Elizabeth Anderson (2010b, 189) closes her book-length argument for racial integration as an imperative of justice with the sobering observation that “the project of integration cannot be left to state initiatives alone. Most of the work of integration inevitably rests with the spontaneous

actions of citizens in civil society.”4 Notice again the gap between this picture and the Institutional View. Contrary to the Institutionalist View’s claim that powerful institutions like the state are “where the action is,” here state action cannot succeed unless ordinary individuals take the necessary actions and develop the necessary attitudes and habits for a truly, not just formally, integrated society (Anderson 2010b, 116). It is tempting to conclude from these considerations that ordinary individuals must also be culpable for their part in structural injustice. Regarding residential segregation, it may be argued that responding to the racial diversification of one’s neighborhood by moving to white enclaves or “white flight” is a culpable behavior for which white individuals bear some responsibility for racial inequality (Kruse 2007). What ordinary individuals do within the remit of their everyday lives is socially consequential, and they should be held responsible for their actions. But the issue is not so straightforward, and this is where the gap between structural injustice and agential wrongdoing begins to appear. Racial hostility is not required for segregated neighborhoods to result from individual residential choices. As Thomas Schelling (1969; 1971) famously demonstrated, segregated neighborhoods can form even when agents navigate a housing market with a preference that at least roughly one out of three neighbors belong to their own racial group, a result that intensifies when the preference is raised to one-half.5 In other words, individuals who are perfectly content to be the racial minority in their neighborhood by a ratio of 2-to-1 end up forming segregated neighborhoods. Racial residential segregation, in principle, need not involve culpable actions like redlining and white flight; surprisingly, it can be the product of many agents acting on what intuitively appear to be innocuous in-group preferences about their neighborhood. The housing market, Schelling (1969, 488) concludes, is “a complex system with collective results that bear no close relation to individual intent.” And as Joseph Heath (2022, 299) observes, if collective results and individual intentions come apart, then “it becomes impossible to say anything about the relative levels of discrimination or tolerance merely from observing the spatial distribution of individuals of different races.” We cannot infer culpable attitudes or actions toward other racial groups from the occurrence of segregation alone. In a complex system, the actions of many agents create emergent properties that are not simply reducible to the properties of the agents that create them. These properties are what license Haslanger’s claim that “society has, so to speak, a life of its own,” thus presenting a distinct object of study—and critique— from the individuals and institutions that comprise it. The basic idea of emergence, often associated with the phrase “the whole is greater than the sum of its parts,” is an old one. Émile Durkheim ([1895] 2013) invoked it to justify social science as a distinctive field of study: society exhibits empirically investigable properties that are not reducible to properties of individuals even though society contains nothing but individuals. But emergence is not specific to sociology. Challenging the purported hierarchy in the natural sciences from (fundamental) physics to (more applied) biology, P. W. Anderson (1972, 393) writes: “The behavior of large and complex aggregates of elementary particles, it turns out, is not to be understood in terms of a simple extrapolation of the properties of a few particles. Instead, at each level of complexity entirely new properties appear.” The concept of structural injustice is premised on a similar claim: the interactions of human agents in a complex society create emergent properties, properties that are not simply reducible to the properties of individuals themselves. While familiar, the basic idea of emergence requires elaboration, for it can be given more and less plausible interpretations. Recent years have seen a proliferation of philosophical accounts of emergence that respond to longstanding worries about its metaphysical and scientific plausibility. For my purposes, it is important to distinguish between two varieties of emergence: ontological emergence and epistemic emergence.6 Each offers a different gloss of the claim that an emergent property of a system is not simply reducible to the properties of its constituent parts. In ontological emergence, an emergent property is metaphysically distinct from its constituent lower-level properties because there are reasons to hold that the property exists in its own right. Such reasons include causal novelty (the emergent property can cause some effect, and this ability is different from even the aggregated causal powers of the lower-level properties) or non-deducibility (the emergent property is not deducible from the lower-level properties even if one knew everything about them). So understood, emergence is heavily criticized for creating more mysteries than it solves: how can something be generated entirely by

lower-level properties, and yet have novel causal powers or be non-deducible from those properties? (Kim 1999). Some deny on these grounds that there are any ontologically emergent properties, pointing to successful reductionist explanations of properties that formerly were considered emergent in the history of science (Graham 2025). Others, such as David Chalmers (2008), argue that there is exactly one plausible instance of ontological emergence: consciousness, as a property not deducible even from complete knowledge of the physical properties of the brain. These criticisms apply to the issue of residential segregation. It seems implausible to say that residential segregation is an ontologically emergent property. Indeed, Schelling’s model shows precisely the deducibility of segregated neighborhoods from the preferences of agents making choices under certain conditions, though the relationship between the individuals and the emergent property is surprising and far from straightforward. That brings us to epistemic emergence. Following Mark Bedau (1997), a property is epistemically emergent insofar as it is deducible from its lower-level properties only by simulation: “set up the system, let it roll, and see what happens.”7 Simulation is required because although the emergent property is fully determined by its lower-level properties, how those lowerlevel properties interact to produce the emergent property is too complex a process to be predictable from knowledge of the lower-level properties. In Schelling’s model, agents following the simple decision rule “Move into a house so long as at least roughly 1/3 of the neighbors are members of my racial group” end up forming segregated neighborhoods, a result that only becomes apparent to us by simulating its implementation. In this epistemic sense, this result is not simply reducible to the actions or intentions of the agents, even if it is their actions and intentions that produced it. The process by which residential segregation is generated by agents’ choices is not explicable by the linear cause-andeffect reasoning that typically suffices in everyday life. My contention is that the kinds of outcomes that plausibly count as structural injustice are epistemically emergent. The concept of structural injustice invites us to look at society as a kind of complex system where multiple overlapping social processes, driven by many agents engaged in economic, cultural, linguistic, and other interactions, produce some vulnerability or deprivation as their emergent outcome. Some social processes, such as economic interactions in a market, are themselves a kind of complex system that produces emergent outcomes—a fact that puts considerable stress on domestically oriented theories of economic justice as well as conceptions of “society” as a closed, self-contained nation-state in an era of globalization. When they have harmful effects on human lives, such outcomes can be described as structural injustice. But in its broadest scope, structural injustice describes the emergent outcomes of multiple overlapping social processes in society: how culture, the economy, politics,

Such outcomes include racial disparities in infant mortality (Wallace et al. 2017), economic inequalities perpetuated by people’s accents (Donnelly, Baratta, and Gamsu 2019), and colonial atrocities like sexual slavery that end up disproportionately impacting poor women (Lu 2017, 128–38). These outcomes are, by nature, not linearly related to or straightforwardly predictable from the actions or intentions of the agents who bring them about. Indeed, the outcome may depart dramatically from what any agent intended or foresaw or could have foreseen. So understood, structural injustice presents a distinct problem from familiar kinds of wrongful individual and institutional actions like exiting a neighborhood out of racial prejudice or depriving a racial minority of equal political status. Such wrongdoings are routinely part of the processes that generate structural injustice, but they will not fully explain the emergent outcome. Indeed, focusing on such wrongdoings would obscure the fact that the outcome can arise without them, as when individuals with integrationist preferences still produce residential segregation. This is true even if wrongdoing is stretched beyond the intentional infliction of harm to the negligent failure to avoid foreseeably causing harm to others, since social interactions may produce emergent outcomes that were unforeseeable to the agents who produced it. In a complex system, it is possible for social interactions to produce vulnerability or deprivation without any agents having acted wrongly. It is this possibility that is foregrounded in Young and Haslanger’s accounts of structural injustice. Notably, Rawls also recognizes this possibility in his discussion of “background justice.” Social processes driven by the actions of ordinary individuals can have inimical results even within a just society: “the conditions necessary for background justice can be undermined, even though nobody acts unfairly or is aware of how the overall results of many separate exchanges affects the opportunities of others” (Rawls 1993, 266). The next line is crucial for understanding Rawls’ point: “There are no feasible rules that it is practicable to require economic agents to follow in their day-to-day transactions that can prevent these undesirable consequences.” In principle, he suggests here, there might be individual-level rules of economic interaction that would fully preserve background justice. But such rules are not relevant in practice due to the epistemically emergent nature of economic outcomes in a market economy: “the rules governing agreements and individual transactions cannot be too complex, or require too much information to be correctly applied” (Rawls 1993, 267). A society’s institutions may conform with Rawlsian principles of justice, but the justice they aim to uphold can erode over time from individual actions that are permitted in those institutions. In short, structural injustice is, at heart, a problem of complexity. This conceptualization of structural injustice bears a strong resemblance to F.A. Hayek’s notion of “spontaneous order,” at least in its ontological and epistemic claims (Hayek 1945; 1967; 1973; 1976; 1979). Hayek himself would deny that emergent social outcomes count as an injustice, as I will discuss in the next

section. While neither Young nor Haslanger reference Hayek’s work, their understanding of structural injustice similarly describes “the result of human actions but not the execution of any human design” (Ferguson 1767, 187). Hayek emphasized the unintended benefits of a market economy as opposed to a planned economy, but complex social processes do not only exist in the market, nor do these processes only produce unintended benefits.8 Playing on “spontaneous order,” structural injustice is an emergent disorder in a complex society.9 Call this the Complexity View. The Complexity View avoids the redundancy challenge: structural injustice does not simply collapse into agential wrongdoing, whether by individuals or institutions. The concept names a distinctive social phenomenon. Before turning to the normative challenge, let me address a potential worry about this view, namely that it is premised on a controversial social ontology involving mysterious “emergent” properties. To the extent that structural injustice can be conceptualized without it, one might argue, the better. That might be true. But it is not a point in favor of the Institutional View. A crucial assumption of that view is that the state and multinational corporations are themselves (collective) agents distinct from the (individual) agents that make them up. Following Christian List and Philip Pettit’s (2011) influential account, the Institutional View claims that collectives or groups are agents when and because they possess the constitutive capacities of agency due to their internal organization and procedures. But group agency itself, it turns out, is an emergent property in the epistemic sense. List and Pettit (2011, 76) write, “While the agency achieved by a group supervenes on the contributions of its members —while it is not ontologically autonomous—it is autonomous in another, related sense. The agency of the group relates in such a complex way to the agency of individuals that we have little chance of tracking the dispositions of the group agent, and of interacting with it as an agent to contest or interrogate, persuade or coerce, if we conceptualize its doings at the individual level.” Although they frame the issues in terms of supervenience and autonomy, the substantive point is that group agency is an epistemically emergent property of a group of individuals organized in a certain way. The Institutional View, then, rests on the acceptance of one particularly striking case of epistemic emergence: group agency. The idea of emergent properties is thus no more mysterious than the idea of treating the state and other institutions as agents in their own right.

An important feature of emergence in the context of social structures is that, ultimately, it is all a product of human agency. As agents, our knowledge of the emergent properties of our actions and our ability to intervene in society in response to them are not static and immutable facts but things that can change and develop over time. The fact that society contains epistemically emergent properties does not make impossible for agents to investigate and intervene in such phenomena as they become known— though it does impose significant limits on how agents can and should engage in such social reform, as the next section will explain. History contains many examples of agents collectively learning to navigate the emergent problems created by their social practices, such as the multiple revisions that economic theory and policy has undergone in the last 100 years in response to various economic crises (Widmaier 2016). Giddens (1990, 38) calls this process of social learning reflexivity: “social practices are constantly examined and reformed in the light of incoming information about those very practices, thus constitutively altering their character.”10 These reforms, he notes, often produce new emergent problems that we could not have foreseen in implementing these new practices, thereby generating new information and starting the cycle anew.11

Agency, understood not as the capacity to prospectively predict and avoid the emergent properties of human action but as the capacity to reflexively examine and respond to them as they arise, is the key to answering the normative challenge. Changes to what we know and can do about an emergent social problem also changes our moral relationship to that problem. In a

complex society, we should expect such changes to be a frequent occurrence. As Seyla Benhabib (2004, 104) observes in the context of burgeoning problems of global justice, “we are constantly being challenged in understanding the moral implications of our actions by discovering unintended consequences…Such knowledge creates moral responsibility.” I argue that there are two plausible and compatible, though independent, explanations of how deontic wrongness is created this way. Hayek overlooks these sources of deontic wrongness. Young also seems to overlook them, leading her to draw an immutable and thus untenable distinction between structural injustice and agential wrongdoing.12

One explanation is what I call the argument from contribution, which builds on some proposals by critics of Young’s distinction between structural injustice and individual wrongdoing (Atenasio 2019; Barry and Ferracioli 2013; Goodin and Barry 2021; Reiman 2012; Sangiovanni 2018). In their view, actions that contribute to producing structural injustice is a form of wrongdoing. This follows from the general principle that one ought not cause, or in collective action cases be part of the cause of, harm to others. There is a difference, however, between acting wrongly and acting culpably. Wrongful actions can be excused and not culpable when performed under certain conditions, including, notably, out of (reasonable) ignorance of their consequences. Those actions are no longer excused and become culpable, however, once this ignorance is dispelled (or is now itself culpable). Combining this with the earlier discussion of epistemic emergence and reflexivity gives us the following picture. Agents are not culpable for producing an emergent outcome, at first. They are excused by their ignorance. But the moral situation begins to change once the harmful outcome has been produced and people are suffering. Claiming ignorance of the harm produced by their social practices becomes increasingly an untenable excuse. The critical mistake in Young’s account is failing to distinguish culpability from wrongdoing: structural injustice that involves no culpable wrongdoing is possible in a complex society, but it is not a permanent condition for agents with the capacity to examine and re-evaluate their social practices in response to emergent problems. This objection raises an important question about collectively produced harms: if the actions of many individuals collectively produce a harm, yet no individual’s action considered on its own makes a difference to that harm, then what, if anything, makes those actions morally wrong? The other explanation of structural injustice’s normative credentials is what I call the argument from passive injustice, building on Judith Shklar’s (1990) influential discussion. Shklar contends that it is a mistake to think that whether something is an injustice depends only on its causal story, such that harmful outcomes that did not originate in wrongful conduct or “active injustice,” including natural disasters, must therefore be mere misfortunes. Equally important is the question of whether agents organized in a political community have the capacity to prevent or mitigate that harmful outcome. Where the capacity exists, it is “passive injustice” for the community to simply let the outcome happen, to be indifferent toward the vulnerable.16 Passive injustice applies to natural and social outcomes alike. Indeed, the fact that humans have repeatedly developed new ways of altering their natural environment should lead us to question the very distinction between what is natural and what is social, and with it, what is inevitable and what is contingent. As she observes, “[s]ome misfortunes of the past…are now injustices, such as infant mortality and famines” (Shklar 1990, 5). SOCIAL REFORM IN A COMPLEX SOCIETY

Recent theoretical challenges, I have argued, pose a dilemma for the concept of structural injustice: either it is distinct from agential wrongdoing but then lacks the normative credentials of injustice, or it is primarily a matter of institutional wrongdoing but then is theoretically redundant. The Complexity View offers a way out. Structural injustice is distinct from (culpable) wrongdoing because predicting the emergent outcomes of human actions is too epistemically difficult, such that structural injustice is not simply a product of (culpable) wrongdoing even though it is ultimately a product of human action. However, structural injustice as emergent disorder is unjust, not merely bad, because we are reflexive agents with the capacity to examine and reform our social practices in light of new information about their effects. Two forms of wrongdoing explain the wrongness of structural injustice: contributing to social processes that harm others, and failing to prevent or mitigate bad outcomes that are socially preventable or mitigable. So understood, structural injustice is a normatively plausible and theoretically valuable concept, one that identifies a distinctive social phenomenon for criticism and redress. One important but easily overlooked implication of this view, however, is that the pursuit of social reform itself faces epistemic limitations in a complex society.23 I will conclude by dwelling on this implication. Goodin and Barry (2021, 343) point out that the very same complexity that distinguishes structural injustice from agential wrongdoing may also threaten the justifiability of holding agents responsible for failing to remedy structural injustice. Structural injustice arises as an unintended consequence of what agents do, but the issue of unintended consequences does not magically disappear when agents introduce social reforms to try to address them. Their key contention and insight is that deliberate and effective social reform is possible even in a complex society so long as agents can imagine and try out alternative social arrangements in response to newfound social problems, learn from their experiences of living with those arrangements, and collectively decide whether the results are sufficiently positive to make those arrangements worth keeping and emulating. Some will object that this approach does not really provide a solution to the problem of unintended consequences so much as simply accept the problem as part of the “process” of social reform. Elizabeth Anderson (2006, 13) writes in her explication of pragmatism: “Unfavorable results—failures to solve the problem for which the policy was adopted, or solving the problem but at the cost of generating worse problems—should be treated in a scientific spirit as disconfirmations of our policies.” But if we are not adept at predicting whether a reform will generate “worse problems,” some will argue, then perhaps it is better not to take the leap at all. Perhaps passivity in the face of structural injustice is not morally wrong but a reasonable response to the potential consequences of intervening in a complex society under deep uncertainty. But this conservative position is not a better answer to the problem of unintended consequences.27 For one, there is no reason to think that the problem of unintended consequences will go away if agents refrain from trying to reform their complex society. Social reform is hardly the only sphere of human activity that generates unintended consequences, as issues like climate change serve to remind us. Nor do we have any reason to expect that reforms will always or even generally lead to worse problems. Such pessimistic expectations are unsupported, as Luban (2020, 78) observes, by “the raw unpredictability implied by the idea of unintended consequences on its own.” Given these facts, the possibility of bad unintended consequences is an acceptable risk for the sake of improving the situation when confronted with real and pressing problems. My point is not that the problem of unintended consequences has no bearing on the pursuit of social reform. Rather, it is that the right response to the problem is not avoiding social reform altogether but managing its risks, for instance, by conducting experiments that limit the number of people potentially affected and that can be halted or reversed (Barrett and Buchanan 2023, 137; Perrow 1999, 304–52; Scott 1998, 345). This may sound like an overly conservative position of its own. But political thinkers of many different stripes have taken the problem of unintended consequences seriously in thinking about how to successfully reform a complex society, even—or especially —when the aim of reform in their view is ultimately to create radically different social arrangements.28 To simply ignore or dismiss the problem would be naïve. Admittedly, these implications of the Complexity View may come across as a disappointment, especially considering the structural injustices of contemporary society. But if the preceding arguments are correct, some

disappointment on this front may be unavoidable if we are to have a compelling explanation of what is distinctive and plausible about the concept of structural injustice. The very issue that distinguishes structural injustice from other wrongs, namely the complexity of contemporary society and the emergent properties of human actions within it, also sets some important, though surmountable, limits on how agents can remedy it. As is often the case, the definition of the problem delimits the contours of the solution. Filling in these contours, of course, will require further, more fine-grained theoretical and empirical work: investigating specific structural injustices, uncovering their origins in complex webs of human action, and discovering latent possibilities for social reform. Still, by probing the concept of structural injustice itself and asking how it may be defended from recent theoretical challenges, we can come to a clearer view of this prominent concern in contemporary politics.
